era: Fuel Subsidies End & Early Unrest (Dec 2025 – Apr 2026)

events.title: Paz Decree Ends National Fuel Subsidies
events.detail: Weeks after taking office, President Rodrigo Paz signed a decree eliminating Bolivia's decades-old fuel subsidies, effectively doubling gasoline prices overnight. The move, intended to relieve strain on dwindling dollar reserves and a collapsing state fuel-import system, became the spark for months of nationwide unrest.

events.title: Law 1720 Allows Land as Loan Collateral
events.detail: The Paz government implemented Law 1720, permitting agricultural land to be used as collateral for loans. Indigenous and agrarian organizations denounced it as a threat to communal and smallholder land tenure, calling it a prelude to land dispossession by lenders.

events.title: COB Declares National General Strike
events.detail: The Central Obrera Boliviana (COB) launched an indefinite general strike backed by more than 70 unions carrying over 100 demands, from a 20% wage increase to opposition to the closure of loss-making state enterprises. The first road blockades appeared in La Paz the same day.

events.title: 67 Highways Blockaded Nationwide
events.detail: Road blockades (bloqueos) spread to roughly 67 highways across Bolivia, choking fuel, food, and medicine supply chains into La Paz and El Alto within the strike's first week.

events.title: Thousands March in La Paz
events.detail: Miners, teachers, Indigenous organizations, and farmers converged on La Paz in a mass march, broadening a strike that began as a labor dispute into a multi-sector movement against the Paz government's economic program.

events.title: Paz Annuls Law 1720; Labor Minister Resigns
events.detail: Facing mounting pressure, President Paz annulled the contested land-collateral Law 1720. Labor Minister Edgar Morales resigned the same day, the first of several cabinet departures during the crisis.

events.title: Miner Delegation Clash Near Plaza Murillo
events.detail: A 20-person COB miner delegation attempted to reach the presidential palace at Plaza Murillo. Miners detonated dynamite and protesters allegedly threw Molotov cocktails; police deployed more than 3,500 officers and used tear gas. More than 5,000 trucks sat stranded on national highways, with losses estimated at $50 million per day.
events.confidenceReason: Government and protest groups dispute who initiated violence at the palace approach.

events.title: Protest Demands Shift to Paz's Resignation
events.detail: As blockades entered their third week, the movement's core demand shifted from sectoral economic grievances to explicit calls for President Rodrigo Paz to resign.

events.title: Evo Morales Leads 190km March Into La Paz
events.detail: Former president Evo Morales led a 190-kilometer march of cocalero and MAS supporters from the Chapare region into La Paz, positioning himself as a central figure in the movement to unseat Paz.

events.title: Cabinet Reshuffle Announced; Colombian Ambassador Expelled
events.detail: Paz announced a cabinet reshuffle (completed by May 25) and expelled Colombia's ambassador Elizabeth García after Colombian President Gustavo Petro voiced support for the protesters, triggering a minor diplomatic rupture.

events.title: Security Forces Open Humanitarian Corridors, Attacked
events.detail: Police and military units opened humanitarian corridors to move stranded food and fuel; convoys were attacked with stones and dynamite. Public Works Minister Mauricio Zamora was ambushed while inspecting a blockade site and had to be rescued by security forces.

events.title: Blockades Spread to El Alto
events.detail: Roadblocks expanded into El Alto, the twin city overlooking La Paz and a historic center of Aymara labor organizing, cutting the capital's main highway links to the altiplano and the rest of the country.

events.title: Paz Relocates to Sucre, Cuts Cabinet Salaries
events.detail: President Paz relocated government operations to the constitutional capital Sucre and announced a 50% salary cut for himself and his cabinet as a gesture of austerity. Evo Morales called for fresh elections within 90 days.

events.title: Congress Authorizes Military Deployment Against Unrest
events.detail: Congress passed legislation authorizing military deployment in support of police operations against the blockades. The same day, counter-protests by shopowners unable to restock their stores broke out, and the government hardened its public tone toward the strikers.

events.title: Paz Signs Military Law: "Time Is Running Out"
events.detail: Paz signed the military-deployment authorization into law and warned publicly that "time is running out" for blockade leaders to stand down, signaling the government's intent to use force to reopen the roads.

era: Escalation, Military Deployment & State of Emergency (Jun 2026)

events.title: FEJUVE Declares El Alto Emergency; Oil Field Occupied
events.detail: El Alto's neighborhood council federation FEJUVE declared a city-wide state of emergency and demanded Paz's resignation. Protesters occupied and set fires at the Humberto Suárez oil field. El Alto Mayor Eliser Roca said the city was losing roughly $6.5 million per day. Defence Minister Marcelo Salinas and Education Minister Beatriz García de Achá resigned.

events.title: Police Retake Oil Facility; 80 Agreements Signed
events.detail: Police regained control of the occupied oil facility, arresting eight. In the Legislative Assembly, the government and various protest sectors signed 80 partial agreements on sectoral demands. Ernesto Justiniano was appointed the new Defence Minister.

events.title: Joint Police-Military Operation on Route 9
events.detail: A joint operation of 900 police officers and 100 soldiers attempted to clear Route 9 between Santa Cruz and Trinidad. The four-hour operation left 6 officers and 14 protesters injured, including 4 hit by gunfire, before security forces withdrew and protesters retook their positions.
events.confidenceReason: Responsibility for the gunfire that injured four people at Route 9 is contested between security forces and protest organizers.

events.title: Chamber of Deputies Permits Direct Military Action
events.detail: The Chamber of Deputies passed legislation permitting the armed forces to take direct action against blockades, rather than a purely supporting role behind police — a significant escalation of the state's response.

events.title: Paz Signs Deployment Bill, Calls Leaders "Narco-Terrorists"
events.detail: President Paz signed the military-deployment bill into law and publicly labeled blockade leaders "narco-terrorists," threatening further escalation. In El Alto, 28 people were arrested after protesters stormed a transport union office.
events.confidenceReason: "Narco-terrorist" characterization is the government's framing, disputed by protest leaders and Evo Morales.

events.title: El Alto Residents Ambush Police Convoy
events.detail: Residents in El Alto ambushed a police convoy, set a vehicle on fire, and forced officers to remove their uniforms in a widely circulated humiliation incident, underscoring the breakdown of state authority in the city.

events.title: 77 Blockades Remain; Tourism Losses Top $200M
events.detail: Seventy-seven active blockades remained nationally (28 in Cochabamba, 20 in La Paz department). Tourism-sector losses from cancellations surpassed $200 million, with roughly 90% of hotel bookings cancelled in affected regions.

events.title: Economic Impact Reaches 5.5% of GDP
events.detail: Cumulative economic losses from six weeks of blockades reached an estimated $2.76 billion, equivalent to roughly 5.5% of Bolivia's GDP, according to government and institutional estimates.

events.title: COB Signals Openness to Direct Talks
events.detail: The COB signaled willingness to negotiate directly with the government for the first time since the strike began. Separately, an "anti-blockade bill" was introduced in the Chuquisaca departmental assembly, reflecting rising public frustration with the disruption.

events.title: El Alto Sub-Mayor's Office Looted and Burned; COB Ultimatum
events.detail: Protesters looted and set fire to the El Alto sub-mayor's office. The COB issued a 48-hour ultimatum demanding Paz's resignation, while Bolivia's constitutional courts ruled the ongoing blockades illegal. Forty-nine blockades remained across five departments.

events.title: Paz Signs Deal With COB
events.detail: President Paz signed an agreement with the COB. Executive Secretary Mario Argollo said, "we must begin to iron out our differences," signaling a partial de-escalation, though other protest groups — including Evo Morales-aligned organizations — refused to join the accord.

events.title: Paz Declares 90-Day State of Emergency
events.detail: On the 50th day of protests, President Paz declared a 90-day nationwide state of emergency and ordered the military to clear remaining roadblocks. More than 200 heavily armed police were deployed to El Alto; the La Paz–Oruro highway was cleared within hours.

events.title: Congress Endorses State of Emergency
events.detail: Congress ratified the 90-day state of emergency. Evo Morales ordered his supporters to lift blockades in Cochabamba, a sign that the largest opposition faction was stepping back from the standoff.

events.title: All Blockades Cleared Nationally
events.detail: All remaining road blockades were cleared nationwide, with only residual debris left on four roads in the Cochabamba–Oruro corridor, ending 53 days of continuous highway disruption.

events.title: Bolivia Floats Currency After 15-Year USD Peg
events.detail: The Central Bank of Bolivia allowed the boliviano to float freely after 15 years pegged to the US dollar. The rate immediately dropped from Bs. 9.73 to Bs. 10.75 per dollar, a formal acknowledgment of the currency's de facto black-market devaluation during the crisis.

events.title: Arrests Reach 583 Nationwide
events.detail: The cumulative number of arrests related to the two-month unrest reached 583 across Bolivia, according to government figures, as prosecutors began opening formal criminal cases against protest organizers.

events.title: Paz Blames State Oil Company Structure for Fuel Crisis
events.detail: President Paz described the structure of state oil company YPFB as an "endemic problem" behind the fuel crisis, shifting blame away from earlier government claims that criminal "mafias" were diverting subsidized fuel for resale.
events.confidenceReason: Government's explanation for fuel shortages shifted over time between blaming diversion "mafias" and YPFB's structural failures.

events.title: Exchange Rate Surpasses Bs. 11 per Dollar
events.detail: The floated boliviano continued to slide, surpassing Bs. 11 per US dollar by July 22 before stabilizing later in the month, deepening cost-of-living pressure on households already hit by fuel price increases.

events.title: Death Toll Reaches 24; 148 Criminal Cases Opened
events.detail: The confirmed death toll from the crisis reached 24, including an estimated 14 attributed to hospitals being cut off from oxygen and medicine supplies during the blockades. Prosecutors had opened 148 criminal cases nationally, 114 of them in La Paz department.
events.confidenceReason: Health Ministry and independent/union sources diverge on how many deaths are directly attributable to blockade-caused hospital shortages versus other causes.

events.title: Bolivia and IMF Reach $1.9B Staff-Level Agreement
events.detail: The IMF and Bolivian authorities reached a staff-level agreement on a 36-month, roughly $1.9 billion Extended Fund Facility aimed at restoring macroeconomic stability, rebuilding reserves, and cutting fiscal and external imbalances. The Fund said the deal could unlock more than $5 billion in additional financing from the World Bank and IDB. It still required IMF Executive Board and Bolivian Congress approval, with no funds yet disbursed.

events.title: Arrest Warrant Issued for Evo Morales
events.detail: Authorities issued an arrest warrant for Evo Morales, alleging links between blockade leaders in San Julián and Cuatro Cañadas and prior land-grabbing cases — a charge Morales rejected as "politically motivated" days earlier when Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo first raised it.
events.confidenceReason: Morales and MAS allies characterize the land-grabbing linkage as a politically motivated prosecution rather than a genuine criminal case.

events.title: Paz Sends Investment Law to Congress
events.detail: President Paz sent an Investment Law to the Plurinational Legislative Assembly, the first in a planned series of market-oriented reforms meant to attract private firms through a more competitive tax and royalty regime, as his governing coalition showed signs of fracturing over the reform agenda.

events.title: Analysts: June Accord "Transferred the Crisis From the Roads to the Calendar"
events.detail: Analysts assessed that the June 20 COB accord did not resolve Bolivia's underlying crisis so much as postpone it, noting the deal left core fiscal, currency, and fuel-supply problems unaddressed while buying Paz political room to pursue IMF-linked reforms.

events.title: Transport Workers, Rural Groups Threaten October Return to Streets
events.detail: Transport unions, rural organizations, and market traders in Bolivia's main cities warned they would resume blockades and protests from October if the government's reform package and unmet economic promises were not addressed, keeping the truce fragile heading into the fourth quarter.

events.title: Paz Marks Independence Day, Declares "A New Bolivia Is Being Born"
events.detail: In a 1-hour-22-minute address from the Casa de la Libertad in Sucre marking Bolivia's 201st independence anniversary, President Paz delivered his first nine-month progress report: the country-risk index falling from roughly 2,200 to 421 points under the floated exchange rate, a $940 million restitution to Bolivians, the expulsion of 17 alleged drug traffickers, and a proposed "national agreement for development." He described the prior administration as having left Bolivia "devastated and dying" and said a "moral transformation" was underway.

media.caption: President Rodrigo Paz addresses Congress from Sucre's Casa de la Libertad on Bolivia's 201st independence anniversary, Aug 6, 2026.

events.title: Government Raises Diesel Price 84% for Large Consumers
events.detail: Supreme Decree 5676 set a new reference price of Bs. 18.00 per liter of diesel for large-volume buyers ("GRACOS," consuming 20,000+ liters/month) and direct clients, an increase of roughly 84% from the prior Bs. 9.80-9.90 rate. The subsidized Bs. 9.80/liter price remains unchanged for transport operators, small businesses, and individual consumers. YPFB president Sebastián Daroca said the two-tier pricing aims to close the arbitrage margin that fueled cross-border diesel smuggling and end shortage-driven queues at filling stations; the agricultural producers' group Codepro rejected the decree and called instead for opening the fuel import market.

media.caption: Fuel pumps in Bolivia amid the diesel supply crunch that prompted the two-tier pricing decree.

events.title: Morales Alleges U.S.-Backed Plot to Kill Him; Justiniano Denies, Demands Proof
events.detail: In a post on X, former president Evo Morales alleged that President Paz and Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano — whom he said had spent roughly two weeks in the United States coordinating with U.S. officials — had ordered an operation in the Chapare region to kill rather than capture him, citing unnamed "patriotic" military and police sources. Morales tied the claim to a separate corruption scandal involving presidential adviser Fernando Cerimedo and demanded the detention of First Lady María Elena Urquidi Barbery over alleged fuel and gold corruption links. Justiniano rejected the accusation as "absolutely false and extremely serious" and challenged Morales to present any evidence to the Public Ministry, noting Morales offered no documentation beyond an unrelated, confirmed meeting between Justiniano and U.S. officials at a Panama anti-cartel summit.
events.confidenceReason: Morales's plot allegation is uncorroborated and explicitly denied by the government; only the underlying dispute over enforcement of his outstanding arrest warrants is independently confirmed.

media.caption: Evo Morales, who alleged a plot against his life from his Chapare stronghold, Aug 20, 2026.

events.title: Presidential Adviser's Ex-Partner Shot Outside Santa Cruz Hotel
events.detail: Two assailants posing as food-delivery couriers fired three shots at Nadia Beller, a lawyer and former congressional candidate, outside a hotel in Santa Cruz de la Sierra. Beller survived and accused her former partner, Fernando Cerimedo — an Argentine political consultant who had worked on Javier Milei's and other right-wing campaigns and whose official credential listed him as President Paz's "principal adviser" despite holding no declared public post — of orchestrating the attack, saying she possessed evidence of corruption reaching the president's family.
events.confidenceReason: Beller's account that Cerimedo ordered the attack over corruption evidence is her own allegation; Cerimedo's precise government role was itself disputed even before the shooting.

media.caption: Nadia Beller, shot outside a Santa Cruz hotel on Aug 17, 2026, accused presidential adviser Fernando Cerimedo of ordering the attack.

events.title: Cerimedo Ordered Into 180-Day Preventive Detention; Government Distances Itself
events.detail: Santa Cruz judge Wilson Espada ordered 180 days of preventive detention at Palmasola prison for Fernando Cerimedo after a six-hour hearing, siding with prosecutors' request over an alternative bid for the maximum-security Chonchocoro facility. Prosecutors presented phone messages allegedly from Cerimedo referencing a need to "eliminate" Beller. The case has embarrassed the Paz government, which for months had presented Cerimedo as a close campaign collaborator; officials now say his digital-communications consulting never amounted to a formal state position.

media.caption: Fernando Cerimedo was ordered held 180 days at Palmasola prison, Aug 21, 2026.

events.title: Legislature Returns Investment Law to Executive Over Blank Page
events.detail: The Plurinational Legislative Assembly sent the 103-article Investment Law project — submitted by the Paz government on Aug 11 to attract domestic and foreign capital via a new National Investment Agency and stricter rules on expropriation — back to the Executive, citing a technical-administrative defect: page 44 of the submitted document was completely blank with no explanation. The Assembly's leadership stressed the observation concerned only the paperwork, not the bill's content, and asked the government to resubmit the missing text as soon as possible.

media.caption: The Legislative Assembly returned the Investment Law bill over a blank page 44, Aug 18, 2026.

events.title: Beller Discharged From Hospital; Prosecutors Order Protection Measures
events.detail: Nadia Beller was discharged from Clínica Las Américas in Santa Cruz after five days of hospitalization for three gunshot wounds, leaving in a wheelchair under police custody. Prosecutor Yolanda Aguilera said the Public Ministry ordered formal protection measures for Beller and that she must give an expanded statement once her health allows, beyond the initial psychologically-supported declaration already taken. "Mi vida sigue en riesgo" ("My life remains at risk"), Beller said on leaving the clinic.

media.caption: Nadia Beller was discharged from hospital under police protection, Aug 23, 2026.

events.title: Two Cerimedo Case Suspects Testify; Prosecutors Seek Their Preventive Detention
events.detail: Colombian national Víctor Hugo C.Z. — identified by investigators as the alleged shooter after initially presenting himself voluntarily to deny involvement — and Róger A.C., accused of supplying the firearm, testified before Bolivian justice authorities. Róger's position worsened after phone-location expert reports reconstructed his movements before the Aug 17 attack. Prosecutors requested 180 days of preventive detention for both, the same term already imposed on Fernando Cerimedo, whom Beller accuses of ordering the shooting.

media.caption: The two co-defendants in the Cerimedo case testified before justice, Aug 24, 2026.

events.title: Paz Dismisses Economy Minister Espinoza After Congressional Censure
events.detail: Congress censured Economy and Public Finance Minister José Gabriel Espinoza on Aug 18 after he skipped a scheduled interpellation on sovereign bond issuances and budget delays, citing prior trips to Santa Cruz and Brazil; 91 of 129 lawmakers present voted to censure him, amid separate questions over an undeclared luxury-vehicle purchase. Paz initially signaled Espinoza might stay in office pending a Constitutional Tribunal review, then reversed course and published a dismissal decree on Aug 21, naming Óscar Mario Justiniano — until then minister of Sustainable Production, Environment and Water — as interim Economy Minister. The government maintains the censure vote itself was unconstitutional, arguing the threshold requires two-thirds of the Assembly's full membership rather than two-thirds of those present.

media.caption: President Paz dismissed Economy Minister José Gabriel Espinoza by decree after a congressional censure vote, Aug 21, 2026.

events.title: Phone Messages Allegedly Link Presidential Intelligence Chief to Beller Shooting
events.detail: Bolivia's Institute of Forensic Investigations (IDIF) extracted chats from Fernando Cerimedo's phone showing a contact saved as "ECG" — whom Nadia Beller and Evo Morales identify as Erik Correa González, the Paz government's intelligence chief — messaging in real time during the Aug 17 attack: "¿le digo que la busquen ahí?" ("should I tell them to look for her there?"), followed by "hermano, en este momento le dispararon, está herida" ("brother, they just shot her, she's wounded"). Investigators also flagged 11 deleted calls between Cerimedo and the same contact that day, plus a message dated Aug 13 that prosecutors say points to premeditation. Beller publicly demanded President Paz break his silence on Cerimedo's role, and she and Morales have called the shooting a "state crime" implicating government and police; no charges have been filed against any official beyond Cerimedo, and the presidency has not directly addressed the ECG identification.
events.confidenceReason: The ECG-to-Erik Correa González identification comes from Beller and Morales, not an independent forensic confirmation, and the government has not addressed it publicly.

media.caption: Fernando Cerimedo. Investigators say phone messages show a contact linked to the government's intelligence chief tracking the Aug 17 attack in real time.

events.title: Cocalero Federations Mount Armed Vigil, Warn Security Forces Over Morales
events.detail: Coca-grower federations loyal to Evo Morales set up a vigil near the Army's Ninth Division in the Trópico de Cochabamba, warning police and soldiers they "will not guarantee" the safety of any officer who tries to "take the life" of Morales or move against the vigil. The mobilization follows Morales's Aug 20 assassination-plot claim and his Aug 23 statement that a colonel had urged him to wear a bulletproof vest permanently because plans against him had moved "beyond a simple detention." Six cocalero federations called a rally for Aug 26 in Ivirgarzama, about 230 km from Cochabamba — with 23 days left before the 90-day state of emergency (declared Jun 20) is due to expire.

media.caption: Evo Morales greets supporters in Ivirgarzama; coca-grower federations mounted an armed vigil in his defense.

events.title: Government Signals Revision to Diesel Price Decree Amid Backlash
events.detail: Facing continued criticism of Supreme Decree 5676 (the Aug 16 measure setting an initial Bs. 18/L reference price for large industrial diesel consumers and direct gas-station sales, an 84% jump from the prior Bs. 9.80/L rate), Deputy Minister of Hydrocarbons Hernán Paredes said the decree "has to be modified" to allow a more competitive diesel price. Proposed changes include broadening which sectors can import diesel directly and pressing state oil company YPFB to raise refinery utilization, currently running at just 18-20% of capacity. The subsidized Bs. 9.80/L rate for transport operators and households remains unchanged.

media.caption: Bolivia's government signaled it would revise the diesel pricing decree after backlash from large consumers, Aug 25, 2026.

events.title: Military Deploys to Santa Cruz as Diesel Blockades Resume in Beni, Oruro
events.detail: Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano ordered a preventive military and police deployment to Yapacaní (131 km from Santa Cruz) on the night of Aug 24-25 after campesino sectors threatened blockades over Supreme Decree 5676's diesel price hike, saying the mission was to "prevent blockades, protect the highway and, above all, avoid confrontations." The threat materialized Aug 26: agropecuario producers from Beni's Marbán province began an indefinite blockade of the Santa Cruz-Trinidad highway at the San Pablo bridge, and quinoa producers blocked the Oruro-Potosí highway with a 48-hour ultimatum, both demanding repeal of the decree. It was the first blockade activity since all roadblocks were cleared on Jun 23, ending a two-month lull.

media.caption: Bolivian security forces deployed near Yapacaní, Santa Cruz, to preempt diesel-decree blockades, Aug 25, 2026.

events.title: Morales Rallies Cocaleros, Calls Paz an "Accidental President"
events.detail: Speaking to hundreds of supporters at a rally in Ivirgarzama, in his Cochabamba Trópico cocalero stronghold, Evo Morales said: "Oportunamente dijimos [Rodrigo Paz] es un presidente por accidente. Ahora se demuestra eso" ("We said early on that Paz is an accidental president. Now that's being shown"), accusing him of corruption and of only knowing how to "steal" rather than govern. Morales also questioned the legitimacy of the state of emergency in effect since June, and union leaders allied with him announced they would seek to coordinate mobilizations with other regions against Decree 5676's diesel price hike.

media.caption: Evo Morales addresses supporters in Ivirgarzama, calling Paz an "accidental president," Aug 26, 2026.

events.title: Two More Detained Over Beller Shooting; Ex-Military Officer Held in Related Enrichment Case
events.detail: A Santa Cruz judge ordered 120 days of preventive detention for Roger A.C. (41) and Paola Andrea V. (39) for "effective complicity in attempted" form, accused of providing and concealing the firearm used against Nadia Beller on Aug 17; the two hired gunmen who fired the shots remain at large. Separately, in La Paz, prosecutors detained Fritz Junior G.A., a former military officer, for 45 days in an illicit-enrichment investigation tied to business dealings attributed to Fernando Cerimedo; security footage showed him fleeing an exchange house where he held legal authority carrying a bag authorities suspect held more than $500,000. It brought to three the number of people detained across the Cerimedo-linked cases, plus Cerimedo himself.

media.caption: Two more suspects were ordered detained in the Beller shooting case, and a third in a related enrichment probe, Aug 26, 2026.

events.title: Government Blames IMF Conditions for Diesel Hike, Rejects Repeal
events.detail: Minister of the Presidency Fernando Aramayo, meeting with President Paz, cabinet members, and municipal mayors, said Supreme Decree 5676 "is one of the conditions we have from the International Monetary Fund ... because it is not sustainable for the State to finance an item that has had a very large corruption component and is bleeding the General Treasury dry," rejecting calls to abrogate the decree. The statement came as rejection of the decree widened: agricultural producers, transport confederations, and rice and sugarcane producers joined peasant organizations in opposing the measure, with Santa Cruz producers giving the government 48 hours to reverse it.

media.caption: Minister of the Presidency Fernando Aramayo defended the diesel decree as an IMF condition and rejected repeal, Aug 27, 2026.

events.title: New Money-Laundering, Narco-Protection Probes Opened Against Cerimedo; Paz Distances Himself
events.detail: Bolivian prosecutors opened two new investigations against Fernando Cerimedo: one for money laundering ("legitimising illicit gains"), opened by Deputy Transparency Minister Yamil García, and one in Beni department for allegedly providing "protection" to "irregular flights" linked to drug trafficking, opened by prosecutor Alexander Mendoza — both stemming from allegations made by Nadia Beller. President Paz responded publicly: "There was never a contract ... there was never a direct working relationship" with Cerimedo, distancing his government from the adviser whose credential had listed him as "principal adviser" to the president.

media.caption: Fernando Cerimedo now faces money-laundering and narco-trafficking-protection probes; Paz denied any formal working relationship, Aug 27, 2026.

events.title: Christian Morales Burgos Sworn In as Permanent Economy Minister
events.detail: President Paz swore in economist Christian Andrés Morales Burgos, previously Vice Minister of Treasury and Public Credit, as permanent Minister of Economy and Public Finance on Aug 25, ending Óscar Mario Justiniano's four-day interim tenure in the post. Paz said Morales had direct knowledge of the government's economic policy and had taken part in recent IMF/World Bank negotiations, tasking him with "consolidating the economic stability achieved" and pursuing $7-10 billion in financing talks. Morales pledged continuity with existing measures, including Supreme Decree 5676, but on Aug 26 said adjustments were needed "to minimize risks" from the producer mobilizations it had triggered.

media.caption: Christian Andrés Morales Burgos sworn in as Bolivia's Minister of Economy and Public Finance, Aug 25, 2026.

events.title: Pro Santa Cruz Civic Committee Gives Government 72-Hour Ultimatum on Diesel Decree
events.detail: Stello Cochamanidis, president of the Pro Santa Cruz Civic Committee, gave the national government 72 hours — until Sunday, Aug 30 — to repeal Supreme Decree 5676, warning that if the deadline passed the Committee's board would meet Monday, Aug 31 to evaluate calling an "Asamblea de la Cruceñidad" to define regional pressure measures. The ultimatum followed an Extraordinary Congress of agricultural producers in Warnes, where the CAO (Agricultural Chamber of the East) said it would formally request the assembly if the decree is not repealed.

media.caption: The Pro Santa Cruz Committee set a Monday, Aug 31 meeting to evaluate convening an Asamblea de la Cruceñidad over Decree 5676.

events.title: Police Clear San Pablo Bridge Blockade, Producers Reblock It Hours Later
events.detail: Police and soldiers cleared the San Pablo bridge blockade in Beni (about 140 km east of Trinidad) on the afternoon of Aug 27, restoring the Trinidad–Santa Cruz route by evening; preliminary, unconfirmed reports put roughly five people injured and a similar number detained in the operation. Marbán province producers, who had held the bridge since the morning of Aug 26 in protest of Supreme Decree 5676, reopened the blockade that same night despite the police action.

media.caption: Police and soldiers cleared the San Pablo bridge blockade in Beni on Aug 27; producers reopened it that night.

events.confidenceReason: Casualty and detention figures from the Aug 27 clearing operation are preliminary and unconfirmed by official sources.

events.title: Diesel-Decree Blockade Spreads to Three Points on Santa Cruz–Beni Highway
events.detail: By Aug 28 the Santa Cruz–Beni highway had three active blockade points — San Pablo bridge, Nueva Jerusalén and Ascensión de Guarayos — as producers kept pressing for repeal of Supreme Decree 5676 despite the active state-of-emergency ban on roadblocks. The regional governor floated setting up a private fuel-distribution alternative to ease supply concerns while the standoff continued.

media.caption: Military personnel guard a Bolivian highway amid the spreading diesel-decree blockades, late Aug 2026.

events.title: Prosecutors Formally Charge Cerimedo With Illicit Enrichment, Seek 6-Month Detention
events.detail: Prosecutor Miguel Cardozo said Fernando Cerimedo gave "evasive" answers under questioning and that the Public Ministry would formally charge him with illicit enrichment affecting the State, requesting six months of preventive detention at the maximum-security Chonchocoro prison in La Paz — a separate case from the attempted-femicide charge over the Aug 17 shooting of Nadia Beller for which he is already jailed. Cerimedo's defense attorney called the enrichment probe "an institutionalized and organized attempted coup d'état" by the La Paz prosecutor's office.

media.caption: Fernando Cerimedo faces a new illicit-enrichment charge and a six-month detention request at Chonchocoro prison, Aug 28, 2026.

events.title: Judge Orders Second Preventive Detention for Cerimedo Over Illicit Enrichment; Clashes With VP Lara
events.detail: After a roughly six-hour virtual hearing, Judge Douglas Borda ordered a second six-month preventive detention against Fernando Cerimedo, this time in the illicit-enrichment case, to be served at the maximum-security Chonchocoro prison in La Paz in addition to his existing detention at Santa Cruz's Palmasola prison over the attempted-femicide case. Cerimedo defended himself during the hearing, saying "I am locked up, your honor, for something that did not occur," and clashed with Vice President Edmand Lara — who took part in the hearing to request his transfer — calling Lara a "mythomaniac" and denying Lara's characterization of him as having wielded major power inside the Executive Branch.

media.caption: Fernando Cerimedo appears at a virtual cautionary hearing from Palmasola prison, Aug 29, 2026.

events.title: Rice Producers Lift San Pablo Bridge Blockade After Provisional Diesel-Supply Deal
events.detail: Producers from Beni's Marbán province lifted the San Pablo bridge blockade on the Santa Cruz-Beni highway early Sunday, five days after installing it on Aug 26, following a provisional agreement with the government. Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano and Beni Governor Jesús Egüez negotiated at the bridge; the government committed to guaranteeing diesel supply for harvest operations and delivered an initial 30,000 liters, with a mobile tanker being coordinated for San Pablo. The deal holds only until Friday, when both sides are due to revisit a substantive solution — Decree 5676 itself remains in place. The final terms cap subsidized Bs. 9.80/L diesel at 120 liters per producer with weekly distribution; Decree 5676's Bs. 18/L tier for large consumers remains unrepealed. Separately, tanker drivers signed their own supply agreement Aug 29 under which YPFB will begin paying down outstanding debts to resume distribution, and other farm towns including San Julián announced their own blockades over the unrepealed decree.

media.caption: Traffic resumes on the Santa Cruz-Beni highway after producers lift the San Pablo bridge blockade, Aug 30, 2026.

events.title: Government Refuses to Repeal Diesel Decree as Civic Committee's Sunday Deadline Passes
events.detail: President Rodrigo Paz told mayors he will not reverse Decree 5676 despite the Comité Pro Santa Cruz's Sunday, Aug 30 deadline to abrogate it. Committee president Stello Cochamanidis had given the government 72 hours from Aug 27 to repeal the decree; with no repeal, the committee's extended board — representatives of 15 provincial sectors, regional blocs, municipalities and neighborhood councils — will meet Monday, Aug 31 at 09:00 to evaluate the government's commitments and decide whether to convene an Asamblea de la Cruceñidad, the body's highest decision-making forum.

media.caption: Comité Pro Santa Cruz president Stello Cochamanidis announces the 72-hour ultimatum on Decree 5676.

events.title: Quinoa Producers Block Oruro-Potosí Highway, Defying State of Exception
events.detail: Organic quinoa producers and truck drivers blocked the Oruro-Potosí highway on Aug 25, breaking the active state-of-exception ban on roadblocks, and gave the government 48 hours to repeal Supreme Decree 5676 and resume subsidized (Bs. 9.80/L) diesel sales in jerry cans at gas stations. Rice and soybean producers in Beni's Marbán province joined the wave of rejection the same day. Producers said the price hike put the planting season at risk of losses up to 70%; National Confederation of Drivers secretary Víctor Tarqui and Marbán rice-farmers' leader Jhonathan Zárate warned of expanded blockades and calls for President Paz's resignation if the decree stood.

media.caption: Producers block a highway over Supreme Decree 5676's diesel price hike, late Aug 2026.

events.title: San Julián Sectors Announce 24-Hour Blockade for Sept. 2 Over Diesel Decree
events.detail: Social organizations, producers and municipal authorities in San Julián (eastern Santa Cruz department) announced a 24-hour road blockade starting midnight Wednesday, Sept. 2, rejecting Supreme Decree 5676 and citing fuel shortages during the ongoing winter sunflower and sorghum harvest. Leaders said the decree's 120-liter-per-month cap on subsidized diesel was insufficient for agricultural operations; the Villa Paraíso federation described the measure as temporary and asked neighboring municipalities to prepare for traffic disruption. Infobae reported Aug 31 that campesino, transport and pro-Morales cocalero sectors more broadly were defying the state of exception, with a separate Cochabamba march by the Seis Federaciones del Trópico planned for Sept. 4.

media.caption: Fuel-shortage protests continue across Bolivia as sectors defy the state of exception, Aug 31, 2026.

events.title: Comité pro Santa Cruz Ratifies Call for Asamblea de la Cruceñidad Over Diesel Crisis
events.detail: The Comité pro Santa Cruz's expanded board met Monday, Aug 31 — after President Paz refused the committee's Sunday deadline to repeal Supreme Decree 5676 — and ratified convening an Asamblea de la Cruceñidad, the region's highest civic decision-making body, to define pressure measures over the diesel crisis. Committee president Stello Cochamanidis said the assembly would build on the Agricultural Chamber of the East's (CAO) congress resolutions and coordinate with the National Civic Movement's planned Sept. 2 meeting; the committee's directive board was set to reconvene Tuesday, Sept. 1 to fix the assembly's exact date. Cochamanidis argued the only lasting fix was for the government to let private companies import and distribute fuel without restriction.

media.caption: Comité pro Santa Cruz ratifies the call for an Asamblea de la Cruceñidad over the diesel crisis, Aug 31, 2026.

events.title: Beni Prosecutors Open Third Cerimedo Investigation Over Alleged Drug-Flight Protection
events.detail: Beni departmental prosecutor Alexander Mendoza opened a third criminal investigation against Fernando Cerimedo, this time in the Controlled Substances Unit, over alleged protection given to irregular flights linked to drug trafficking through the Santa Ana de Yacuma municipality — small aircraft suspected of landing on clandestine runways after transporting cocaine. Mendoza said the case, which follows the femicide and illicit-enrichment probes, could expand to implicate other private citizens or officials as evidence emerges. Cerimedo remains jailed at Santa Cruz's Palmasola prison and, since Aug 29, under a second preventive-detention order for La Paz's Chonchocoro facility.

media.caption: Fernando Cerimedo faces a third investigation, over alleged drug-trafficking links, Aug 30, 2026.

events.title: Beller Prepares Testimony Alleging Fuel-Diversion Scheme Implicating First Lady, Gold Smuggling
events.detail: Protected witness Nadia Beller prepared a statement to La Paz prosecutors alleging Fernando Cerimedo partnered with First Lady María Elena "Bibi" Urquidi in a scheme diverting roughly 2 million liters of subsidized YPFB diesel a day onto the black market, generating an estimated $84,000-150,000 daily depending on the outlet's accounting. Beller further alleged Cerimedo was linked to a July 23 attempt to smuggle 189 kilograms of gold (valued at roughly $25 million) out of Viru Viru airport via a courier detained with falsified Dubai-bound documents, and to drug-trafficking flights in Beni involving tampered radar transponders. The presidency did not address the specific allegations but reiterated it would not interfere in the investigation. These are unverified, contested claims from a single witness in an ongoing criminal case, not established findings.

media.caption: Nadia Beller prepares new allegations against Cerimedo naming the First Lady, Aug 30, 2026.

events.confidenceReason: Allegations from a single protected witness in an active criminal case; not independently corroborated, and outlets report inconsistent dollar figures.

events.title: Police Commander Sokol Resigns Amid Audio-Leak Corruption Probe; Álvarez Takes Over
events.detail: General Mirko Sokol resigned as Commander General of the Bolivian Police after nine months in the post, amid a prosecutorial investigation into a leaked audio in which he allegedly referenced a roughly $2 million collection among senior officers to manipulate promotions and the police command succession. Sokol had built his tenure around a "zero tolerance" anti-corruption pledge and the March capture of Uruguayan drug trafficker Sebastián Marset. President Paz swore in Colonel Adrián Javier Álvarez Arismendi, previously head of the Police's national technology directorate and former El Alto police chief, as interim Commander General the same day at the Palacio Quemado, alongside Roger Roca Saavedra as interim sub-commander and Franz Williams Cabrera Quispe as interim inspector general.

media.caption: General Mirko Sokol resigned as Bolivia's Police Commander General amid a corruption audio-leak probe, Aug 31, 2026.

events.title: Arrest Ordered for Alleged Beller-Shooting Coordinator, Ex-Customs Chief With Prior Drug Conviction
events.detail: Santa Cruz prosecutors ordered the arrest of María Argentina Rojas Roca as an alleged accomplice in the Aug 17 attempted murder of Nadia Beller, accusing her of meeting with and transferring money to the men identified as the gunmen. Rojas Roca is a former head of Customs at Santa Cruz's Viru Viru airport despite a prior drug-trafficking conviction and deportation from Brazil in January 2021; Beller has linked her to Alberto Soto, a former Customs chief she also identifies as part of Fernando Cerimedo's circle. The order widened the criminal case beyond Cerimedo, who remains jailed, and the two men already charged as accomplices.

media.caption: María Argentina Rojas Roca, former Viru Viru Customs chief, was ordered arrested over the Beller shooting, Aug 31, 2026.

era: Crisis Resumes: YPFB Intervention, Santa Cruz Blockades & VP Break With Paz (Sep 2026)

events.title: Government Issues Decree 5698, Raising Subsidized Diesel Cap for Small Producers to 2,500 Liters
events.detail: President Paz promulgated Supreme Decree 5698, letting small agricultural producers registered in the Unified Agricultural Regime (RAU) or holding a Tarjeta de Control buy between 121 and 2,500 liters of diesel per month at the subsidized Bs. 9.80/liter price by presenting only their ID card or the Tarjeta, up from Decree 5676's 120-liter monthly cap. Bolivia's tax service will send the National Hydrocarbons Agency a monthly list of RAU-registered producers to enable their IDs at the pump; fuel must be for own consumption. The measure responded to small-producer complaints that Decree 5676's original cap was too low for the winter sunflower and sorghum harvest, though it left the decree's Bs. 18/liter large-consumer tier unchanged.

media.caption: Decree 5698 raises the subsidized-diesel purchase cap for small agricultural producers to 2,500 liters a month, Sept 1, 2026.

events.title: VP Lara Publicly Breaks With Paz Over Cerimedo, Cites Forensic Evidence
events.detail: Vice President Edmand Lara escalated his public break with President Paz, telling Argentine television that forensic analysis of Fernando Cerimedo's devices showed "sustained contact" with the men accused of shooting Nadia Beller, and that he had personally seen Cerimedo "give orders and instructions to the ministers" from inside the government. New photographs published by Beller appeared to corroborate the account: one, dated May 2026, shows Cerimedo at a desk on the 23rd floor of the presidential headquarters in La Paz; another places him within Bolivia's official delegation at a March 7, 2026 meeting between Paz and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Cerimedo has denied the claims, saying he never attended cabinet meetings and "has not given orders to ministers." The episode deepened the rift between Paz and Lara, a former police officer who has criticized the government's fuel-subsidy removal since early in the administration.

media.caption: Photographs published by Nadia Beller purport to show Fernando Cerimedo working from Bolivia's presidential headquarters, Sept 1, 2026.

events.confidenceReason: Lara's account and Beller's photographs are contested by Cerimedo, who denies giving orders to ministers or influencing government decisions; no independent forensic verification has been published.

events.title: Paz Government Places State Oil Company YPFB Under Intervention
events.detail: President Paz signed Supreme Decree 5697 placing state oil company YPFB under "extraordinary, transparent and temporary" state intervention for up to 180 days (extendable once by 90), forming a commission of the ministers of Economy and Public Finance, Sustainable Production/Environment/Water, Hydrocarbons and Energy, and Public Works to audit the fuel import and distribution chain. The government said the goal was to recover YPFB's operational efficiency and trace smuggling, diversion and stockpiling networks blamed for chronic diesel and gasoline shortages; Bolivia imports roughly 60% of its gasoline and 95% of its diesel, spending an estimated $90 million a week. The decree states it does not dissolve YPFB or alter its legal status.

media.caption: Government of Bolivia decrees intervention of state oil company YPFB, Sept 2, 2026.

events.title: New Blockades Erupt at Four Points in Santa Cruz Over Diesel Decree
events.detail: Producers and social organizations installed blockades before dawn at San Julián, Yapacaní, Cuatro Cañadas and Los Troncos in Santa Cruz department, cutting the Santa Cruz–Beni highway, the route to the Chiquitanía, and the Yapacaní–Cochabamba road. The action, agreed at a weekend assembly for an initial 24 hours, again targeted Supreme Decree 5676's Bs 18/liter diesel price for large consumers; Santa Cruz's Terminal Bimodal suspended most departures to Cochabamba, La Paz, Oruro and Beni as a result. Police mobilized tactical and riot units toward the blockade points but had not moved to clear them as of this update; some organizers broadened their demands to include President Paz's resignation.

media.caption: New blockades cut Santa Cruz department highways over the diesel decree, Sept 2, 2026.

events.title: Supreme Electoral Tribunal Launches Electoral Reform Process
events.detail: Bolivia's Supreme Electoral Tribunal and its nine departmental tribunals opened formal discussions in Cochabamba on electoral-system reform, covering the electoral roll, electoral justice, political representation, and transparency controls. The initial phase is meant to produce an internal roadmap before the dialogue expands within weeks to political organizations, journalists, Indigenous peoples, and civil society — a process launched independently of, but running alongside, the diesel-decree and Cerimedo crises.

events.title: Lara Files Criminal Complaint Against First Lady and Cerimedo Over Police Commander's Removal
events.detail: Vice President Edmand Lara's legal team filed a criminal complaint with the Public Ministry against First Lady María Elena "Bibi" Urquidi and Fernando Cerimedo for six alleged offenses: aggravated influence trafficking, misuse of influence, criminal association, organized crime, state-damaging contracts, and illicit enrichment of private individuals affecting the State. The complaint is based on an audio in which a voice attributed to Urquidi asks Cerimedo to help remove then-Police Commander General Mirko Sokol at the request of a man identified only as "Miguelito" — whom Lara says is Miguel Rockholt Montaño, a figure with a drug-trafficking record who was reportedly being investigated by anti-narcotics officers under Sokol's command. In the recording, Cerimedo — describing Sokol as "useless" — commits to arranging his removal. Lara's team requested forensic, acoustic and phonetic analysis to authenticate the recording and identify the voices; Sokol resigned Aug 31.
events.confidenceReason: The audio's authenticity is pending forensic, acoustic and phonetic verification; neither the First Lady nor Cerimedo has publicly confirmed the recording.

media.caption: VP Edmand Lara filed a criminal complaint against First Lady María Elena Urquidi and Fernando Cerimedo over Police Commander Sokol's removal, Sept 1, 2026.

events.title: San Julián, Cuatro Cañadas Blockades Lifted After Deal; Yapacaní Holds Out
events.detail: Producers lifted the San Julián and Cuatro Cañadas blockade points after reaching an agreement with the government, while the Yapacaní blockade on the Cochabamba–Santa Cruz road continued. Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano traveled to Cuatro Cañadas with YPFB technicians to explain Supreme Decree 5698's expanded 2,500-liter subsidized-diesel allowance for small producers as the basis of the deal. Decree 5676's underlying Bs. 18/liter large-consumer tier remains unrepealed, and the Los Troncos point's status was not confirmed in the agreement.

media.caption: Producers lifted blockades in San Julián and Cuatro Cañadas after a deal on DS 5698; Yapacaní's blockade continued, Sept 3, 2026.

events.title: Lara Releases Second Audio Allegedly of Paz and Cerimedo Plotting State-of-Exception "Narrative"
events.detail: Vice President Edmand Lara publicized a second purported audio recording, this one allegedly of President Paz and Fernando Cerimedo discussing how to build a public "narrative" for applying the state of exception ultimately decreed June 20 to end the May-June blockades. Lara said the recording would be sent to the Public Ministry for expert authentication, and that if genuine it would show Cerimedo in contact with Paz days before the decree and with a larger governing role than publicly acknowledged. Asked by reporters about the audios' authenticity, President Paz declined to comment: "Let Justice act, let it do its work; I don't pay attention to audios, I do pay attention to what Justice and those who conduct the expert review can determine."
events.confidenceReason: The recording's authenticity is unverified and pending expert forensic review; President Paz declined to confirm or deny it.

media.caption: VP Edmand Lara presents a second purported audio of Paz and Cerimedo discussing the state-of-exception "narrative," Sept 3, 2026.

events.title: Thousands of Cocaleros March in Cochabamba, Defying State of Emergency
events.detail: Thousands of coca growers and other Morales-aligned social sectors marched from Avenida Petrolera to central Cochabamba, defying the active state of emergency to demand repeal of Supreme Decree 5676 and greater fuel supply. It was the first cocalero march since the 53-day blockades of May-June. Police did not intervene and the march was peaceful; Evo Morales, evading his outstanding arrest warrant from the Chapare, urged supporters to march but did not attend himself. Cocalero leader Isidro Auca, heading the column, said: "This government wants to raffle off our natural resources, it doesn't listen to the people. We will not allow further damage to the economy, this is a warning, we will continue the struggle."

media.caption: Coca growers march toward central Cochabamba in defiance of the state of emergency, Sept 4, 2026.

events.title: Protected Witness Beller Alleges Cerimedo/Urquidi Fuel-Diversion, Gold-Smuggling and Drug-Trafficking Network
events.detail: Nadia Beller, testifying as a protected witness to La Paz prosecutors in the illicit-enrichment case against Fernando Cerimedo, alleged he and First Lady María Elena Urquidi participated in a scheme diverting roughly 2 million liters of fuel a day from state oil company YPFB onto the black market, generating an estimated Bs. 1 million (~$84,000-150,000) daily. Beller also linked Cerimedo to a July 23 attempt to fly 189 kilograms of gold (~$25 million) out of Viru Viru airport in suitcases bound for Dubai, seized when 22-year-old Adrián Lema Roca was stopped, and to a suspected cocaine-trafficking network using clandestine airstrips in Beni department. No charges have been filed over these specific allegations; Beller remains under witness protection at an undisclosed location following the Aug. 17 shooting she attributes to Cerimedo.
events.confidenceReason: Allegations from a single protected witness relayed via prosecutorial sources; not yet tested in court or independently corroborated.

media.caption: Fernando Cerimedo faces new fuel-diversion, gold-smuggling and drug-trafficking allegations from protected witness Nadia Beller.

events.title: Marbán Producers Lift San Pablo Bridge Blockade (Beni) After Diesel-Supply Deal
events.detail: Farmers from Marbán province, Beni, lifted their blockade of the San Pablo bridge on the Trinidad-Santa Cruz highway after four days, following a police withdrawal and reopening on Aug. 28 and a government pledge to supply subsidized diesel at Bs. 9.80/liter capped at 120 liters with weekly distribution for the province. Supreme Decree 5676's Bs. 18/liter rate for large consumers remains unrepealed. Evo Morales later cited the episode (Sept. 12) as evidence the state of exception was not being enforced, saying Defense Minister Justiniano negotiated directly with blockaders rather than using security forces to clear the route.

media.caption: Dialogue reopens at the San Pablo bridge blockade in Beni, Aug 29, 2026.

events.title: Lara Proposes Paz as a Witness in the Cerimedo Case, Challenges Him to a Face-to-Face
events.detail: Vice President Edmand Lara announced he will formally propose President Rodrigo Paz as a witness before the Public Ministry in the Cerimedo investigation, so Paz can state under oath what he knows about the disputed audio recordings and his relationship with Cerimedo. Lara said he is "willing to a confrontation [careo] with the president, face to face, for him to tell me it's a lie that Fernando Cerimedo was his advisor," and said he personally witnessed Cerimedo giving orders and instructions to ministers in two cabinet meetings. Paz has not accepted the challenge; he previously said he would leave the disputed audio to the justice system to evaluate.

media.caption: VP Edmand Lara proposes President Paz as a witness in the Cerimedo case and challenges him to a face-to-face confrontation, Sept 8, 2026.

events.title: Deputies' Justice Commission Unanimously Backs 3-Month State-of-Exception Extension
events.detail: The Plural Justice Commission of the Chamber of Deputies unanimously approved (of members present) a chamber resolution to extend the state of exception, due to expire Sept. 18, by 90 more days. Deputy Manolo Rojas said there is "a latent risk against democracy" and "a group waiting for the 18th of September to convulse the country again." The resolution directs Chamber President Roberto Castro to ask Vice President Lara to convene the full Plurinational Legislative Assembly to consider it; the extension still requires floor votes in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Assembly, and opposition legislators have signaled likely rejection, arguing the government failed to resolve the underlying crisis during the initial 90 days.

media.caption: Deputies' Justice Commission unanimously backs a 90-day extension of the state of exception, Sept 10, 2026.

events.title: Santa Cruz Moto-Taxi Federations Call Off Planned Indefinite Blockade After Overnight YPFB Talks
events.detail: Seven moto-taxi federations across Santa Cruz department had set an indefinite blockade for 9:00 a.m. Sept. 11 at 13+ points — Warnes, Satélite Norte, Doble Vía La Guardia, Cotoca, Pailón, Cuatro Cañadas, San Julián, Guarayos, San Javier, Concepción, La Guardia, Samaipata and Mairana — demanding regular fuel supply, no price increases, outstanding compensation payments and resolution of pending YPFB cylinder paperwork. After overnight talks with Hydrocarbons Minister Marcelo Blanco and YPFB, federation leaders called off the blockade, but organizers described it as a "recess" rather than a resolution and set Oct. 10 as their checkpoint to reassess.

media.caption: Moto-taxi federations set up blockade points across Santa Cruz department before calling off the action, Sept 11, 2026.

events.title: Evo Morales Says State of Exception Is Effectively Defunct, Warns Extension Would Be "Worse"
events.detail: Evo Morales said the state of exception is no longer being applied, arguing Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano "is disregarding" it because the government negotiated directly with Marbán producers over the San Pablo bridge blockade in Beni instead of deploying police or military to clear it. Morales called the measure ineffective and warned that extending it for three more months, as the Deputies' Justice Commission proposed Sept. 10, would be "worse."
events.confidenceReason: Reflects Evo Morales's characterization of enforcement; government has not directly responded to the "disregarded" framing.

media.caption: Evo Morales says the state of exception is no longer being enforced and warns extending it would be worse, Sept 12, 2026.

events.title: Central Bank Dollar Sales Pull Official Exchange Rate Back From Record Bs. 12.64
events.detail: The Central Bank of Bolivia's official dollar rate hit a new record of Bs. 12.64 around Sept. 9-10 before falling for three straight sessions — Bs. 12.42 (Sept. 10), Bs. 12.04 (Sept. 11) and Bs. 11.53 (Sept. 12) — after the BCB temporarily suspended new dollar-purchase operations (Sept. 7), created a Restricted Monetary Reserve under Resolution RD Nº 131/2026 (Sept. 8), and began direct dollar distribution to private financial-system entities (Sept. 9) to ease what it called "unnecessary shocks" in the currency market.

media.caption: BCB dollar sales pull the official exchange rate back from a record Bs 12.64, Sept 12, 2026.

events.title: Paz Reactivates Cochabamba and Santa Cruz Refineries, Authorizes Crude Imports to Lift Diesel Output
events.detail: President Paz's cabinet approved Supreme Decree 5701, exceptionally authorizing YPFB's refining subsidiary YPFB Refinación S.A. to import crude oil and process it at the Gualberto Villarroel refinery in Cochabamba and Guillermo Elder Bell refinery in Santa Cruz, which Paz visited Sept. 9 to relaunch fuel production. The government said importing roughly 10,000 barrels of crude per day would lift domestic gasoline production from 27% to 40% of demand and diesel from 5% to 8% within a year, with jet fuel rising from 81% to 100%. The measure follows weeks of hours-long lines to load diesel and gasoline across La Paz, Santa Cruz, and Cochabamba that persisted into early September despite the YPFB intervention (Decree 5697, Sept. 2).

media.caption: President Paz at the Gualberto Villarroel refinery in Cochabamba as the government relaunches domestic fuel production, Sept 9, 2026.

events.title: Nadia Beller Expands Declaration, Alleges Cerimedo Coordinated With Security Forces
events.detail: Nadia Beller, the lawyer shot in the Aug. 17 attack she attributes to ex-partner Fernando Cerimedo, expanded her declaration before Bolivian prosecutors on Sept. 9, alleging that Cerimedo "coordinated with law enforcement forces" (coordinaba con fuerzas del orden) during his informal role advising President Paz. The statement builds on her Aug. 30 testimony describing a YPFB fuel-diversion and gold-smuggling network and adds detail on Cerimedo's asserted links to Bolivia's security apparatus, which Beller's legal team says corroborates the influence-trafficking complaint VP Lara filed against Cerimedo and First Lady Urquidi on Sept. 1.
events.confidenceReason: Beller's allegations are sworn testimony to prosecutors but remain unproven claims pending judicial investigation.

media.caption: Fernando Cerimedo and Nadia Beller, whose Sept 9 expanded declaration alleges Cerimedo coordinated with security forces.

events.title: Prosecutors Summon Beller and Businessman Jofré Azzarini for Advance-Proof Testimony in Cerimedo Case
events.detail: La Paz departmental prosecutor Luis Carlos Torres confirmed the Public Ministry summoned Nadia Beller and businessman Robin Luis Jofré Azzarini as witnesses in the illicit-enrichment and money-laundering case against Fernando Cerimedo. Because Beller cannot travel to La Paz for health reasons stemming from the Aug. 17 shooting, her testimony will be taken via an advance-proof procedure (prueba anticipada) in Santa Cruz the following week, with support from the Santa Cruz regional prosecutor's office. Separately, Beller confirmed the same week that she will also testify Sept. 23 before an Argentine prosecutor as a witness in an unrelated corruption case involving Argentina's disability agency (ANDIS), where Cerimedo is also implicated.

media.caption: Nadia Beller, summoned Sept 12 for advance-proof testimony in the Cerimedo case.

events.title: Government Announces Decree to Extend State of Exception 90 Days as Legislative Opposition Grows
events.detail: Interior Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo announced in Cochabamba on Sept. 13 that the executive will send the Plurinational Legislative Assembly a new decree extending the state of exception — in effect since June 20 under Decree 5636 and due to expire Sept. 18 — by 90 more days, citing "gran consenso ciudadano" and the risk of renewed mobilizations and blockades. The announcement follows the Chamber of Deputies' Plural Justice Commission's Sept. 10 unanimous resolution recommending the extension, which the Commission said was needed because "still exists the risk of new mobilizations and blockades that could affect the country's stability." Opposition mounted quickly: the Senate's Libre bloc said it would oppose the measure, and the National Congress of Free Transport rejected it, arguing a state of exception "should not be used to limit social protest." The resolution still needs a floor vote in the full Chamber of Deputies followed by a joint session with the Senate, expected the week of Sept. 14; Evo Morales had separately argued Sept. 12 that the state of exception was already going unenforced at blockade sites like San Pablo bridge.

media.caption: Government pushes a 90-day state of exception extension as legislative opposition grows, Sept 14, 2026.

events.title: Prosecutors Add Usurpation-of-Functions and Money-Laundering Charges Against Cerimedo
events.detail: Attorney General Roger Mariaca announced Sept. 9 that the Public Ministry expanded its illicit-enrichment investigation into Fernando Cerimedo to include usurpation of public functions and money laundering (legitimación de ganancias ilícitas), saying a prosecutorial commission would take an expanded statement from him "within other criminal facts attributed to the defendant." The additions bring Cerimedo's concurrent legal exposure in Bolivia to four cases — illicit enrichment/money laundering, attempted femicide against Nadia Beller, domestic violence, and the Beni drug-trafficking-flights probe opened in late August — while he remains held at the high-security Chonchocoro facility after being transferred from Palmasola.

media.caption: Fernando Cerimedo now faces usurpation-of-functions and money-laundering charges alongside his existing cases, Sept. 9, 2026.

events.title: Regulator Authorizes YPFB to Import and Sell Diesel Directly for a Year
events.detail: The National Hydrocarbons Agency (ANH) issued Administrative Resolution RAR-ANH-DJ-UGJN N.° 0625/2026, authorizing state oil company YPFB to import and commercialize diesel oil for its own service stations nationwide for one year — fuel arriving by tanker truck to YPFB Logistics storage plants across departments, each shipment requiring a Certificate of Quality of Origin under Supreme Decree 5619, with monthly volume reporting to the ANH. The authorization follows the Sept. 2 intervention of YPFB (Decree 5697) and gives the state company a direct import channel intended to ease the diesel shortages that have driven blockade threats since August.

media.caption: YPFB was authorized to directly import and sell diesel for a year, Sept. 12, 2026.

events.title: Cabinet Formally Approves Decree 5707 Extending State of Exception; COB Calls It "an Attack on Democracy"
events.detail: President Paz's cabinet formally approved Supreme Decree 5707 on Sept. 14, extending the state of exception in force since June 20 by 90 more days "while risk factors persist," Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano said, adding, "Esperamos que el Congreso apruebe este decreto para que podamos ampliar" the emergency measures. The decree moved beyond the Chamber's Sept. 10 committee recommendation to a formal executive act requiring the Legislative Assembly's absolute-majority approval before the original 90-day term lapses around Sept. 18-19. COB executive secretary Mario Argollo called an extension "un atentado a la democracia" ("an attack on democracy"), warning "no podemos vivir en una dictadura en un país democrático," while political blocs remained split — Súmate and a PDC faction signaled likely support, Libre said its vote would hinge on the government first justifying the measure's results.

media.caption: Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano confirmed the cabinet's approval of Decree 5707 extending the state of exception, Sept. 14, 2026.

events.title: Lara Convenes ALP Session on Extension as CSUTCB Declares "Permanent Mobilization"
events.detail: Vice President Edmand Lara convened the Legislative Assembly's Seventeenth Ordinary Session for Wednesday, Sept. 16 at 16:00 to consider Decree 5707. The same day, the Evo Morales-aligned peasant confederation CSUTCB declared itself "en estado de emergencia y movilización permanente" against the extension, arguing it would deepen protest criminalization and entrench authoritarian measures, and set a national "Evo Pueblo" assembly for Sept. 26 in Lauca Ñ to define its response. Former president Jorge Tuto Quiroga separately urged the government to first report the state of exception's results before seeking a new term, warning the extension risked delaying constitutional-reform debate; COD Chuquisaca also rejected the measure.

media.caption: Vice President Edmand Lara convened the Assembly to consider the state-of-exception extension, Sept. 15, 2026.

events.title: Government Floats Possible State of Siege as Legislature Prepares Extension Vote
events.detail: As the Legislative Assembly prepared to vote Sept. 16 on the 90-day state-of-exception extension, presidential spokesperson José Luis Gálvez said the government could go further and declare a state of siege (estado de sitio) — potentially including curfews restricting public circulation — if new road blockades materialize: "Si se ve pertinente imponer otras medidas, lo vamos a hacer, la ley lo contempla." Officials cited the risk of a repeat of the May-June blockades that killed at least 16 people and cost over $3 billion, led by the departmental peasant federations and COB with Morales-aligned support, as justification for keeping escalation options open even as the current measure's legal basis was still being debated in Congress.
events.confidenceReason: The state-of-siege option is the government's stated contingency, not an announced or activated measure as of Sept. 16.

media.caption: Presidential spokesperson José Luis Gálvez said a state of siege remains an option if blockades resume, Sept. 16, 2026.

events.title: COB and FENCOMIN Reject Extension, Each Announce a National Assembly
events.detail: Hours before the Legislative Assembly's vote, COB executive secretary Mario Argollo reappeared publicly to reject the 90-day extension of the state of exception, arguing "no existe justificativo legal para prolongar el Estado de Excepción" since the country had been calm for three months, and blaming the government for pinning the fuel crisis on "los 53 días que ha estado movilizado el país." Argollo said the COB would convene a national assembly (ampliado nacional) to evaluate progress from the joint working committees set up with the Executive after the May–June blockades, without setting a date, and warned that extending the measure would be politically "negativo" for President Paz. The mining-cooperative federation FENCOMIN separately rejected the extension the same day, with president Josué Caricari calling it a "mordaza" (gag) and "persecución," and likewise announced its own national assembly without fixing a date.

media.caption: COB executive secretary Mario Argollo rejected the state-of-exception extension and announced a national assembly, Sept. 16, 2026.

events.title: Legislature Approves 90-Day Extension of State of Exception, 100-58
events.detail: The Plurinational Legislative Assembly's session, convened by VP Edmand Lara at 16:00 on Sept. 16, ran past 01:00 on Sept. 17 before approving Decree 5707's 90-day extension of the state of exception in force since June 20, with 100 of 158 legislators (122 deputies and 36 senators participating) voting in favor against 58 opposed — 21 more votes than the required threshold. Government Minister Marco Oviedo and Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano argued the restrictions were needed to head off a reactivation of destabilizing blockades across roughly 20 economically linked conflict points in eight departments, while opposition figures aligned with Evo Morales, including floor questions of "¿para qué 90 días más?", argued no active blockade justified the measure. Protesters gathered peacefully at the Casa Social del Maestro near Plaza Murillo under police watch during the session; no clashes were reported.

media.caption: The Legislative Assembly's overnight session approved the 90-day extension of the state of exception, 100-58, Sept. 16-17, 2026.

events.title: Senate Activates Six-Member Special Commission to Investigate Cerimedo Corruption Allegations
events.detail: The Chamber of Senators formally activated a special investigative commission into corruption allegations tied to Fernando Cerimedo and his role within the Executive branch, giving it a three-month mandate to report findings to the full Senate. The six-member, three-party panel comprises Paola López and Marcelino Flores (PDC), Leonardo Roca and José Sánchez (Libre), and Eliana Acosta and Marcelo Cardona (Unidad). Its mandate covers Nadia Beller's public allegations linking Cerimedo to suspected fuel, diesel and gold-smuggling operations and to unnamed presidential associates, alongside the separate criminal cases already underway (attempted femicide, illicit enrichment, domestic violence, usurpation of functions and money laundering).

media.caption: The Senate activated a six-member special commission to investigate corruption allegations tied to Fernando Cerimedo, Sept. 18, 2026.

events.title: Nadia Beller Testifies for Three Hours, Seeks Protected-Witness Status
events.detail: Nadia Beller testified for roughly three hours before Bolivia's Public Ministry in a Gesell chamber at Santa Cruz's Special Victims Unit, answering close to 100 questions from prosecutors followed by cross-examination from Cerimedo's defense team, as part of the illicit-enrichment case. She formally requested entry into the protected-witness program, citing fears for her safety, and said the armed attack against her on Aug. 17 was aimed at preventing "la denuncia de presuntos hechos de corrupción." A virtual hearing was scheduled for Sept. 19 at which prosecutors planned to request seizure of Cerimedo's digital devices.

media.caption: Nadia Beller testified for roughly three hours and requested protected-witness status, Sept. 18, 2026.

events.title: Congress Ratifies $1.9B IMF Financing Deal
events.detail: The Chamber of Deputies approved the Extended Fund Facility financing law on Sep 18 with support well above two-thirds, and the Senate sanctioned it the next day, Sep 19, via a waived-procedure vote (Law 723), completing congressional ratification of the 36-month, SDR 1.369 billion (~$1.9B) IMF program first agreed at staff level on Jul 29. Terms: up to 10-year repayment per disbursement, amortization starting after a 4.5-year grace period, and a variable interest rate of 3.47% tied to SDR rates. The deal still requires final approval from the IMF's Executive Board, expected around Oct 2, with a first disbursement of roughly $250 million anticipated shortly after.

media.caption: Bolivia's Senate ratifies the $1.9 billion IMF financing agreement, Sept. 19, 2026.

events.title: Paz Eliminates Diesel Subsidy Entirely via Decree 5716; Price Jumps 83%
events.detail: Hours after Congress ratified the IMF financing deal, President Paz announced in a recorded early-morning message the total elimination of Bolivia's diesel subsidy, effective the next day (Sat., Sep 20) under Supreme Decree 5716. The two-tier pricing set by Decree 5676 (Bs. 9.80/L for transporters and individual consumers, Bs. 18.00/L for large-volume "GRACOS" buyers) was replaced with a single international-reference price of Bs. 17.95/L for all consumers — an increase of roughly 83% for previously subsidized buyers. The government said the subsidy had cost about $55 million per week and fueled cross-border smuggling; Paz said "Se acabó el negocio de los delincuentes, subvención o futuro yo elijo futuro" ("The criminals' business is over — subsidy or future, I choose future"). Compensatory measures announced alongside the decree: an expanded PEPE cash-bonus program reaching roughly 2.9 million recipients (about $79 million) and Bs. 800 million in preferential credit for transport operators and small merchants. A decision on gasoline subsidies was deferred.

media.caption: Diesel pumps in Bolivia after Decree 5716 eliminated the fuel subsidy, raising the price 83% to Bs. 17.95/liter, Sept. 19-20, 2026.

events.title: COB, Transport Unions and Producers Reject "Dieselazo," Threaten Blockades
events.detail: Sectors nationwide rejected Decree 5716's diesel-price hike (dubbed the "dieselazo"). The COB rejected the decree and convened an undated national emergency assembly (ampliado) to define protest measures, saying the government is "the only responsible party for social instability" for breaking prior agreements under a state of exception that formally bars blockades and strikes. The Confederación de Choferes (transport drivers), led by Secretary General Víctor Tarqui, declared its own state of emergency and set a national assembly for Monday, Sep 21 to decide on measures; La Paz's interprovincial transport federation separately announced a departmental road blockade starting that same Monday. Tanker-truck operators (cisterneros) suspended fuel loading and unloading operations indefinitely pending resolution, and agricultural producers in Yapacaní, Santa Cruz — the site of earlier August blockades over the GRACOS diesel tier — symbolically burned copies of the decree at an emergency sector meeting. The Hydrocarbons, Presidency and Economy ministers said they remained open to dialogue with any sector that requested it.

media.caption: COB mobilization coverage as the labor confederation convenes a national emergency assembly over the diesel decree, Sept. 19-20, 2026.

events.title: Interdepartmental Transport Leaders Walk Out of Talks, Confirm 24-Hour National Strike
events.detail: Leaders of Bolivia's interdepartmental bus and freight transport sector abandoned talks with government ministers held at YPFB facilities, saying the government came with no fare-adjustment proposals to offset Decree 5716's diesel-price hike. "No ha habido ningún diálogo, no han venido con propuestas" ("There has been no dialogue, they haven't come with proposals"), said Evert Chino, an interdepartmental transport leader. The sector confirmed a 24-hour nationwide stoppage for Monday, Sep 21, warning it could extend to 48 or 72 hours if the government did not respond, despite the state of exception's bar on blockades and strikes.

media.caption: Interdepartmental transport leaders after walking out of talks with government ministers over the diesel price hike, Sept. 20, 2026.

events.title: YPFB Rules Out Gasoline Price Hike, Warns Against Speculation
events.detail: State oil company YPFB said the elimination of the diesel subsidy under Decree 5716 does not affect gasoline, which remains at its regular commercial price of Bs. 6.96/liter, and guaranteed continued production, distribution and sale of gasoline for private, public and industrial vehicles. YPFB asked the public not to fall for speculation or misinformation that could cause unnecessary crowding at filling stations, after diesel's price jumped 83% to Bs. 17.95/liter over the weekend.

media.caption: YPFB says gasoline prices are unaffected by the diesel subsidy's elimination and warns against speculative hoarding, Sept. 20, 2026.

events.title: Government Reaches Deal With Santa Cruz Transport Federations, Averts Monday Stoppage
events.detail: After the Federación Departamental de Transportistas de Ómnibuses de Santa Cruz had announced suspending interprovincial, interdepartmental and international bus departures over Decree 5716's diesel-price hike, government ministers Mauricio Zamora (Public Works) and Ernesto Justiniano (Defense) met that evening in Santa Cruz with Fedetrans, the Federación 16 de Noviembre and the Federación Departamental, alongside YPFB refinery manager Jorge Paniagua and departmental transport director Wilfredo Rey, to explore ways to shield passenger fares from the diesel increase. The sides agreed to keep talks open and ruled out a Monday work stoppage; Justiniano said the government would allow peaceful demonstrations but warned "si es necesario el uso de la Policía y de los militares, lo haremos" against any attempt to block routes. Santa Cruz transport service ran normally on Sep 21.

media.caption: Government ministers negotiate with Santa Cruz transport federation leaders over diesel pricing, averting a Monday stoppage, Sept. 20-21, 2026.

events.title: Police and Military Deploy on Three Highways to Preempt Diesel Blockades
events.detail: Police and Armed Forces personnel deployed Monday to Villa Remedios on the La Paz–Oruro highway, plus the Oruro–Cochabamba and El Alto–Tiquina routes, under the expanded state of exception, to guard against anticipated blockades by transport and social sectors opposed to Decree 5716's diesel-subsidy elimination.
